newsitem.title: UK: Britons flex spending power at major supermarkets.
newsitem.headline: Britons flex spending power at major supermarkets.

text.p: Britain's leading four supermarkets appear to be increasing market share as incomes rise and shoppers switch from smaller, cheaper chains and high street stores, analysts said on Wednesday.

Shares in Safeway, one of the big four along with Tesco, J. Sainsbury and ASDA, leapt on Wednesday after it said current sales were up 4.6 percent and had risen 4.7 percent in the year to March 29. This allayed fears that it was losing market share to Sainsbury.
"There is still more opportunity for the big four to increase volumes in the market," Safeway chief executive Colin Smith told a news briefing.

Analysts had worried that Safeway might suffer as Sainsbury pushed for sales growth. Sainsbury's current sales gained 4.2 percent over a year ago compared with a four percent increase at the start of the year.
Market leader Tesco appears to be maintaining growth of around six percent.
Safeway's statement on Wednesday put paid to that concern and a relieved market pushed its shares up 25 pence to 356 pence by 1505 GMT.
"There is share to go for, there is an awful lot of business out there to be taken," said Richard Perks, analyst at Verdict Research.
Verdict estimated that the big four held around 44 percent of the market -- which includes groceries, chemist items, newsagents goods and drinks -- during 1996.
The losers in this market share battle appear to be second and third tier supermarkets and analysts point to rising wages for the switch.
Shares in high street discounter Kwik Save, which said last week that current sales were falling six percent, tumbled 13.5 pence on Wednesday to 267 pence.
Analysts said rising real earnings could be prompting shoppers to move away from discounters to seek service and quality at the big four.
"Real wages are growing strongly and we think the typical Kwik Save shopper feels inclined to trade up and maybe make a trip to Tesco," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
Figures out on Wednesday showed that average British earnings were up 4.5 percent in the year to March compared with a three percent gain a year ago.
At the same time, supermarkets are reporting flat or falling prices, particularly in fresh produce, which is also helping to attract shoppers, analysts said.
"Incomes are at very strong levels and there is deflation. Suddenly, the big four supermarkets are looking attractive to shoppers who maybe had to stick to bargains before," the analyst added.
Although the supermarket leaders aim to be competitive on price over a range of goods, discounters can often undercut, particularly on specific products.

Verdict's Perks also noted growth in non-food sector sales for part of the rise in turnover for the market leaders. "There is a chunk of growth from non-foods which these companies may be picking up," he said.
Supermarkets sell clothing, entertainment products such as compact discs and videos, along with newspapers, magazines and tobacco, widening their competition targets.

Perks cautioned that high street chains such as W H Smith and Woolworths, part of the Kingfisher group, which sell a limited range of music and entertainment along with newspapers, could suffer from the growing volumes of the supermarkets.
But he added that it was not clear how sustainable growth would be for all four of the market leaders.
"I am a little surprised that they are all doing so well at the same time. Maybe that is unsustainable," he said.
